Farthing
FAR-þHING
n.
Middle English ferthing, a fourth-part; the smallest English coin (one-fourth of a penny). The KJV uses farthing for two different small Greek coins: the Roman quadrans (one-fourth of an as; 1/256 of a denarius—Matt 5:26; Mark 12:42) and the Greek assarion (1/16 of a denarius—Matt 10:29; Luke 12:6).

📖 Biblical Definition

The farthing in the KJV renders two different small coins of the first-century Roman world: the quadrans (one-fourth of an as, approximately 1/256 of a denarius, the smallest copper coin in everyday circulation) and the assarion (a small bronze coin worth 1/16 of a denarius). Both are small denominations, used in the Gospels to illustrate either the smallest unit of debt or the cheapest of items. The supreme uses are several. Matthew 5:26: Christ’s warning at the end of the Sermon on the Mount’s anger-and-reconciliation passage: verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing. The context is the man who has angered his brother and not been reconciled; if the matter reaches the magistrate, the debt-prison will hold him until the entire debt is paid down to the smallest copper. The reference is rhetorical: the smallest farthing is the lowest unit, the absolute exact-and-complete amount. Mark 12:42 (paralleled in Luke 21:2): the widow’s two mites which make a farthing—the smallest two coins available, which together made the smallest copper coin in higher denomination. Matt 10:29 and Luke 12:6: are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. The sparrows here are sold at the cheapest possible rate—two birds for a small bronze coin—and Christ’s teaching is that even at this nearly-worthless commercial valuation, the Father’s providence extends to every individual bird; how much more then to His children. The biblical doctrine of the farthing therefore has structural pastoral substance across multiple registers. First, the legal-debt register: the uttermost farthing must be paid; God’s justice is exact and complete, and the debt of sin is not partially-paid but fully-paid (Christ’s cry It is finished [tetelestai, paid in full] is the gospel-answer to the demand for the uttermost farthing). Second, the small-gift register: the widow’s two mites totaling one farthing is measured by Christ as more than the rich men’s substantial gifts because of the proportion and cost (her gift was all she had, theirs was overflow). Third, the providence register: the sparrows sold for a farthing are individually known to the Father, and the saint’s value to Him is incomparably greater. The smallest coin in everyday circulation becomes, in Christ’s hands, the carrier of teaching that ranges from the exactness of divine justice to the tenderness of divine providence over every detail of the saint’s life.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FARTHING as the fourth of a penny; the smallest English coin; in scripture, the KJV uses it for two different small Greek coins (quadrans and assarion), each illustrating either the smallest debt-unit (Matt 5:26) or the cheapest commercial valuation (Matt 10:29).

expand to see more

FARTHING, n. — The fourth of a penny; a small copper coin of Britain. In scripture, the KJV uses farthing for two distinct small Greek coins: the Roman quadrans (1/256 denarius) and the Greek assarion (1/16 denarius).

PENNY, n. — A small English coin, equal to four farthings. In scripture, the KJV uses penny for the Greek denarius (Matt 20:2; Mark 6:37; etc.).

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 5:26 — "Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing."

Matthew 10:29 — "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father."

Mark 12:42 — "And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing."

Luke 12:6 — "Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The farthing-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the loss of the small-coin precision in modern translations (which often substitute the colorless cent or penny for the KJV’s farthing, losing the carefully-distinguished quadrans-vs-assarion of the original), and by the consequent loss of the structural pastoral substance that runs through the small-coin uses across the Gospels.

expand to see more

Modern translations have generally simplified the small-coin vocabulary, substituting cent, penny, or generic small coin for the KJV’s careful farthing, mite, penny, pound, stater, etc. The simplification is grammatically defensible (modern English does not maintain a precise multi-tier hierarchy of small coins as the first-century Roman East did) but pastorally costly. The KJV’s farthing covers two distinct Greek coins (quadrans and assarion) at carefully-distinguished biblical moments; the loss of the precision flattens what Christ’s teaching is doing. The uttermost farthing of Matt 5:26 carries a force the colorless last penny equivalents miss; two sparrows for a farthing of Matt 10:29 carries the precise rate the modern equivalents soften. The recovery is the recovery of the precision: read the KJV with attention to its careful coin-vocabulary, and the pastoral substance the small-coin teaching carries comes through with full force.

The structural pastoral substance that runs through the small-coin uses is itself worth noting. Christ’s use of the smallest coins-of-everyday-life as the carriers of teaching about divine justice (the uttermost farthing of exact reckoning), divine providence (the sparrows the Father sees fall), and disciple-faithfulness (the widow’s two mites worth more than the rich men’s talents) is itself a deep pattern. The kingdom of heaven values rightly what the world values cheaply; the smallest coin matters in the divine accounting; the smallest gift, given in faith from the smallest means, is weightier in heaven than the largest gift given from abundance. The recovery of the small-coin teaching is therefore the recovery of an entire register of Christ’s pastoral instruction—a register that the modern simplification of vocabulary has often quietly muted.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kodrantēs (quadrans, 1/256 denarius—Matt 5:26; Mark 12:42) and assarion (1/16 denarius—Matt 10:29; Luke 12:6); both small coins of first-century Roman Palestine, used by Christ as carriers of teaching on divine justice, divine providence, and disciple-faithfulness with what is humanly counted small.

expand to see more

Greek kodrantēs (G2835) — quadrans, the smallest Roman copper coin (Matt 5:26; Mark 12:42).

Greek assarion (G787) — assarion, a small bronze coin (Matt 10:29; Luke 12:6).

Greek lepton (G3016) — mite, the smallest coin (Mark 12:42, two mites make one farthing).

Greek dēnarion (G1220) — denarius, one day’s wage (the larger denomination against which farthings and mites are measured).

Usage

"Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing—the exactness of divine justice in Matt 5:26."

"Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father—the tenderness of divine providence over what the world counts cheap."

"Modern translations flatten the small-coin vocabulary; recovery of the KJV’s precision (farthing, mite, penny, stater) restores the pastoral substance Christ’s teaching carries through the small-coin uses."
